tip: Τα μαλλιά (ta maliá) = hair – normally plural in Greek: μακριά μαλλιά (makriá maliá) = long hair.
Μοιάζω σε (miázo se) = take after; σε and τον merge into στον: μοιάζει στον παππού (miázi ston papú) = he's like his grandpa.
Ο/η συνάδελφος (sinádhelfos) = colleague – the same form covers men and women.
Συνάδελφος plus μου gains a second accent: συνάδελφός μου (sinádhelfós mu) = my colleague.
Ο φίλος της (o fílos tis) = her boyfriend – context tells you when it means more than just a friend.
Κανένας (kanénas) = anyone in questions, no one in negatives: κανέναν (kanénan) does both jobs here.
Σκέφτομαι συχνά (skéftome sikhná) = I often think – the -μαι (-me) ending looks passive but the meaning is active, like θυμάμαι (thimáme = I remember).
Σκεφτόμαστε να (skeftómaste na) = we're thinking of – σκέφτομαι plus να introduces the plan you have in mind.
Time-when normally needs no preposition: το μεσημέρι (to mesiméri) = at midday, just article plus noun, like το βράδυ (to vrádhi) = in the evening.
Φοβάμαι (fováme = I'm afraid) takes a plain object, with no of: φοβάται το σκοτάδι (fováte to skotádhi) = she's afraid of the dark.
Μη before a verb = don't: μη φοβάσαι (mi fováse) = don't be afraid.
Τα γενέθλια (ta yenéthlia) = birthday – the word is always plural in Greek.
Πριν από (prin apó) = ago: πριν από μία ώρα (prin apó mía óra) = an hour ago.
Το τραπέζι (to trapézi) is both the table and a dinner party, so στο τραπέζι (sto trapézi) here means coming to the meal, not the furniture.
Ελάτε (eláte) = come, to a group or as the polite form; έλα (éla) to one friend.
Μεγαλύτερος (meghalíteros) = older, and with the article it's the oldest: ο μεγαλύτερος (o meghalíteros).
Μεγαλώνω (meghalóno) covers both growing up and raising someone: μεγάλωσα (meghálosa) = I grew up.
Πολλή (polí) is the feminine form of much: πολλή αγάπη (polí aghápi) = a lot of love; πολύ sounds the same but is the neuter and the adverb.
Η νονά (i noná) = godmother, ο νονός (o nonós) = godfather: της νονάς μου (tis nonás mu) = my godmother's, and they usually count as close family in Greece.
Ο κουμπάρος (o kumbáros) = the best man – he normally stays honorary family for life in Greece.
Ελεύθερος (eléftheros) = free, and it's also the everyday word for single.
Μόνη της (móni tis) = on her own; the ending shifts with the person: μόνος μου (mónos mu) = on my own.
Τώρα πια (tóra pia) = these days, not anymore – it signals that something has changed.
Professions normally come with no word for a: είναι αστυνομικός (íne astinomikós) = he's a police officer.
Εργάζεται (ergházete) = she works, from εργάζομαι – a notch more formal than δουλεύω (dhulévo).
Χρειάζεται να (khriázete na) = needs to – χρειάζομαι (khriázome) takes the -μαι (-me) endings that look passive but mean I need.
Naming uses τη λένε (ti léne = they call her): την κόρη μας τη λένε Ελένη (tin kóri mas ti léne) – the daughter is named twice, as κόρη and as τη.
Η νύφη (i nífi) = the bride, and the same word covers daughter-in-law and sister-in-law.
Οι δικοί μου (i dhikí mu) = my folks, my own people – warm and very common in speech.
Name-day custom: friends drop in uninvited – ανοιχτό σπίτι (anikhtó spíti) = open house.
